question: According to the World Health Organization (WHO), what is the primary focus of palliative care?

options.B: Improving the quality of life of patients and families facing life-threatening illness
options.C: Hastening the dying process in hopeless cases
options.D: Exclusively providing end-of-life care in specialized hospices

explanation: Palliative care focuses primarily on improving the quality of life for both patients and their families when facing life-threatening illnesses. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h1)

question: When should palliative care ideally be introduced in the disease trajectory?

options.A: Only in the final twenty-four hours of life
options.B: After all curative options have completely failed for six months
options.C: Early in the course of illness, often alongside life-prolonging treatments
options.D: Exclusively after a patient is discharged from the hospital

explanation: Modern palliative care is designed to be introduced early in the illness trajectory and can run concurrently with disease-modifying treatments. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h1)

question: In palliative care, who is considered the primary unit of care?
explanation: Palliative care treats the patient and family as a single unit of care because serious illness affects the entire support system. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h2)

question: Why is cultural sensitivity important when applying palliative care principles in Nigeria?

options.A: Because medical equipment is identical across all Nigerian cultures
options.B: Because family structures and religious beliefs heavily influence health decisions
options.C: Because Nigerian law forbids the use of pain medications
options.D: Because cultural beliefs have no impact on patient comfort

explanation: Cultural structures, community expectations, and religious beliefs shape how Nigerian patients and families view and make decisions about health and illness. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h2)

question: What is the primary objective of curative treatment?

options.A: Providing psychological counseling to the family
options.B: Eradicating the disease or halting its progression
options.D: Ensuring a peaceful death in a hospice

explanation: Curative treatment aims strictly at eradicating the disease or halting its progression to restore normal function. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h3)

question: How can palliative care and curative treatment relate to each other in modern practice?

options.A: They must never be administered at the same time
options.B: Palliative care can be provided concurrently with life-prolonging curative treatments
options.C: Curative treatment must always follow palliative care
options.D: Palliative care replaces curative treatment only in pediatric wards

explanation: Palliative care is frequently introduced early and can run concurrently with life-prolonging or curative treatments. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h3)

question: Who originally coined the concept of 'total pain' in palliative care?
explanation: Dame Cicely Saunders formulated the total pain concept to describe pain's physical, psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why is it insufficient to treat only the physical dimension of pain in palliative care?

options.A: Because analgesics are illegal in many hospitals
options.B: Because pain is purely a spiritual phenomenon
options.C: Because unresolved psychological, social, or spiritual distress can worsen overall suffering
options.D: Because physical pain always resolves spontaneously

explanation: Total pain is multidimensional; ignoring psychological, social, or spiritual distress will leave the patient's overall suffering unaddressed. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is a key role of the nurse within the multidisciplinary palliative care team?

options.A: Acting as central coordinator and primary advocate for the patient
options.B: Replacing the physician in prescribing all major surgeries
options.C: Isolating the family from the rest of the healthcare team
options.D: Focusing solely on administrative hospital duties

explanation: Nurses frequently serve as the central coordinators, maintaining continuous contact and advocating for the patient within the multidisciplinary team. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary approach necessary in palliative care?

options.A: It reduces the total number of hospital staff needed
options.B: It addresses the complex physical, emotional, and social needs of the patient effectively
options.C: It eliminates the need for patient and family communication
options.D: It ensures that only doctors make decisions about comfort

explanation: A multidisciplinary team brings together diverse expertise to address the wide-ranging physical, psychological, and social needs of patients. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h5)

question: What is a recommended approach when communicating with patients and families in cultures where discussing death is sensitive?

options.A: Force the patient to talk about death immediately
options.B: Ignore the family and speak only to hospital administrators
options.C: Navigate conversations with tact and involve trusted family spokespersons or elders when appropriate
options.D: Avoid discussing any aspect of the illness entirely

explanation: Sensitivity to cultural norms, such as involving trusted family spokespersons or elders, is essential when discussing difficult topics. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is a primary benefit of effective patient and family-centered communication in palliative care?

options.A: It speeds up hospital discharge paperwork
options.B: It builds trust and empowers patients to participate in care planning
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for pain medications
options.D: It prevents family members from asking questions

explanation: Clear, empathetic communication builds trust, reduces anxiety, and empowers patients to be involved in decisions about their care. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h6)

question: What does the ethical principle of non-maleficence mean in the context of end-of-life care?

options.A: Doing no harm and avoiding burdensome, futile medical interventions
options.B: Ensuring the patient receives maximum financial profit
options.C: Following every family command regardless of patient wishes
options.D: Mandating aggressive surgical intervention for all terminal cases

explanation: Non-maleficence requires healthcare providers to do no harm, which includes avoiding burdensome and futile interventions at the end of life. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h7)

question: What is a common ethical and clinical challenge regarding pain management at the end of life in Nigeria?

options.A: An oversupply of opioid medications in every clinic
options.B: Opiophobia and strict regulations surrounding opioid use
options.C: Patients refusing any form of comfort care
options.D: The complete absence of physical pain in terminal illness

explanation: Opiophobia (fear of addiction) and strict regulations often impede adequate pain management at the end of life in resource-constrained or restrictive environments. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T2#GNS321_U4_T2_h7)
